newsitem.title: PERU: Peru frees first innocent prisoners in new scheme.
newsitem.headline: Peru frees first innocent prisoners in new scheme.

text.p: The Peruvian government on Tuesday named the first innocent prisoners to be freed on the recommendation of a new body created to speed the release of those jailed unjustly on charges of terrorism.

A decree, published in the government daily El Peruano, awarded pardons to three journalists, Jesus Alfonso Castiglione, Eduardo Sihue Cano and Jose Antonio Alvarez Pachas on the same date Peru celebrates national journalists' day.
Justice Minister Carlos Hermoza Moya said on local radio he expected more releases to be announced this week because the special body had recommended pardons for 31 prisoners.
In August Congress passed a law setting up a commission with powers to recommend to President Alberto Fujimori pardons for innocent prisoners sentenced by Peru's "faceless" military courts.
As part of a tough anti-guerrilla strategy Fujimori introduced in 1992 a secret military court system, where anonymous judges usually wore hoods when passing sentence.
He argued the courts were necessary because civil judges were failing to convict terrorists through incompetence, corruption or fear.

However, with the diminishing threat from the country's guerrilla groups - the Shining Path and the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) - the military courts have come under increasing criticism.
Since the beginning of 1995 the government has freed about 150 prisoners convicted of terrorism but human rights groups said another 750 were still imprisoned unjustly.

Under current legislation the secret courts are due to end their functions on October 15, but a string of top government officials - including congressional president Victor Joy way - have publicly called for an extension to the system.
